item.title: Mainstream Open Source Licenses: From MIT to AGPL, How Engineers Choose
item.description: In September 2017, React switched overnight from BSD+Patents to MIT. The reason: the Apache Software Foundation put React’s license on its “do not depend on” list, and Automattic (WordPress’s parent) immediately announced it would stop rewriting its UI on React. Facebook couldn’t withstand the ecosystem pressure and folded. Seven years later, in March 2024, Redis moved its core from BSD 3-Clause to a dual RSALv2+SSPL license — within a week AWS, Google, and Oracle jointly forked Valkey to replace it.

item.title: From Redis Switching to BSL to the AGPL Revival: Source Available, AI, and the License Wars
item.description: In August 2023, HashiCorp moved Terraform, Vault, Consul, and all its core products from MPL 2.0 to BSL 1.1. The community erupted; a month later the Linux Foundation spearheaded a fork called OpenTofu. You’d think the story ends there — but in April 2024 IBM announced a $6.4 billion acquisition of HashiCorp, closing in February 2025, making HashiCorp a business unit under IBM’s Red Hat. The license-changing OSS company didn’t decline; it became an acquisition target.

item.title: SD/TF Card Selection Guide — Read the Specs, Match the Scenario
item.description:
Same Card, Different Device, Different Fate

The same model of TF card might die in two weeks inside a surveillance camera but run fine for six months in an action cam. The difference isn’t the brand — it’s the write workload. Surveillance is 24/7 continuous sequential writes. Action cameras do intermittent burst writes. Raspberry Pi system disks do random small-file writes. Three completely different demands on the flash memory.

item.title: USB Flash Drive Selection — Controller, NAND Grade, and Interface, Not Just Capacity and Read Speed
item.description:
The Three Components of a USB Flash Drive

A USB flash drive has the same hardware structure as an SD/TF card: flash die + controller + interface. The difference is that SD card controllers are potted and firmware-locked by the card maker, leaving the parameters opaque, while USB drive controllers and die grades are relatively open and verifiable with tools.

The common failure mode of cheap USB drives is a stripped-down controller. A sub-1-yuan Alcor or Solid State System chip with no real wear leveling or ECC, paired with black-grade reclaimed NAND. Every flash cell loses a bit of life each erase cycle; without a controller to absorb the failures, bad blocks spread into the data area within weeks.

item.title: SSD Selection — Form Factor, Protocol, and NAND, From SATA to PCIe 5.0 NVMe
item.description:
The Gap Between Sequential Peaks and Real Workloads

SSD advertised speeds are sequential read/write peaks, but common workloads like system disks and app launches are bottlenecked mainly by 4K random I/O. Upgrading from SATA to PCIe 3.0 NVMe is a qualitative change, but going from PCIe 4.0 to 5.0 produces little perceptible difference for boot times or daily app responsiveness; the benefit shows up mainly in large sequential transfers (VM images, video footage).

item.title: HDD Selection — The CMR vs SMR Core Distinction, and NAS, Surveillance, and Enterprise Tiers
item.description:
The Cost Advantage of HDDs for High-Capacity Storage

A 1TB NVMe SSD costs around 400 yuan today, with a small price gap against a same-capacity HDD. But above 16TB, HDD per-GB cost is about 1/5 to 1/10 of SSD. Scenarios such as NAS, cold backup, surveillance recording, and video archiving — high-capacity, low-frequency access — remain the most economical choice for HDDs.

The key distinction in HDD selection is CMR vs SMR: choosing wrong causes large drops in NAS sync performance and abnormally long RAID rebuild times. This post covers that distinction first, then moves on to RPM, helium filling, and product tiers.

item.title: Embedded Camera Module Selection Handbook — From Basics to Purchasing Reference
item.description:
About This Handbook

This handbook covers 20 mainstream embedded camera modules — 8 OV/GC series (OV2640, OV5640, OV7725, GC0309, OV7670, OV3660, GC2053, GC4653) and 12 Sony IMX/OV MIPI series (IMX219, IMX273, IMX296, IMX307, IMX335, IMX415, IMX477, IMX678, IMX708, IMX766, plus OV9281 and OV5647). All parameters are sourced from official datasheets, with sources noted at the end of each section.
